items.claim: A redirect parameter whose value must resolve to a path on the application's own origin is not an open redirect; the finding requires the attacker to control the destination origin, not merely the path or the query string that follows the application's own host.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the value is resolved by a client rather than the server — a protocol-relative value, a scheme-relative or backslash-normalised form, or a value that a downstream client (email client, chat renderer, mobile deep-link handler) reinterprets as absolute — because the server-side check passes while the user agent still leaves the origin.

items.claim: An open redirect is proved by a 3xx response whose Location header resolves to an attacker-controlled origin, captured with the redirect not followed; the presence of a `next`, `returnUrl` or `redirect` parameter on a request that returned 200 proves nothing.
items.disproof: The claim is false when the response cannot be observed with its headers intact — a fetch-based client, a proxy that rewrites 3xx, or a headless browser configured to follow redirects — in which case the Location must be captured from a raw exchange or from the browser's network log, and a screenshot of the final page is insufficient evidence.

items.claim: An open-redirect defence that inspects the destination with a real URL parser and compares the host is bypassed by any implementation that does a substring, suffix or endsWith test on the raw string, because a value such as an attacker host whose name merely contains the allowed host, or an allowed host with a trailing credential-holding prefix, satisfies the substring test while resolving elsewhere.
items.disproof: The rule is false when the check parses with a WHATWG-compatible URL constructor and compares the parsed host for exact equality, because the confusable forms then fail to match and no substring confusion is possible; a check that also rejects relative and scheme-relative input closes the remaining variants.

items.claim: An authorization server answering with a `redirect_uri_mismatch` error has refused the unregistered destination, so that exchange is the authorisation server's defence working and must not be reported as an open redirect on the client.
items.disproof: The rule is wrong when the client is the component at fault — it holds a pre-registered wildcard or prefix pattern that the server honours, so an attacker's host matches a registered pattern and the code is returned to it — or when the mismatch is only for the tested variant while a weaker registered form still accepts the malicious origin, in which case the server's exact-match rule is not what stopped the attack.

items.claim: The consequential open-redirect evidence is the post-authentication hop — the redirect that fires after a real login or token grant, not a bare redirect on an unauthenticated entry point, because the pre-auth redirect carries no session while the post-auth one lands the user on the attacker's page already carrying a fresh session.
items.disproof: The claim is false when the pre-auth redirect is itself the finding — for example it feeds a `Referer`-based reset or a state parameter that the attacker can poison, or it is on a page that performs an authenticated action before redirecting — in which case the unauthenticated redirect is independently exploitable and its severity does not depend on a completed login.
